Where it began

Varun Aaron was born in Jamshedpur on 29 October 1989. He went to Loyola School in his home city and later studied at JAIN (Deemed-to-be-University). His cricket grew through the Jharkhand under-19 side and then the MRF Pace Foundation, where young Indian quicks learn their trade.

He first played first-class cricket for Jharkhand in the 2008–09 Ranji Trophy, at home to Jammu and Kashmir, and took two wickets in each innings. It was a tidy start, and a sign of the pace to come.

The player

What set him apart was speed. In the 2010–11 Ranji season he took 13 wickets and was timed at 153.4 km/h, the kind of figure that makes selectors sit up. A tour of Australia with India's Emerging Players in 2011 went well, and that October he made his one-day debut for India. His first Test followed the next month.

He played nine Tests between 2011 and 2015 and took 18 wickets, with a best of 3 for 97. In one of his early one-day games, at Eden Gardens against England, he bowled only three overs but found time to bowl Alastair Cook, a wicket that mattered to India. He came back to the one-day side in January 2014 after two years away.

What made him special

Fast bowling is hard work, and he did it at full tilt. Batsmen facing him knew the ball would arrive in a hurry. Across his first-class career he took 173 wickets.

With the bat he was not one for the long innings. His 35 Test runs came at 3.89, with a highest score of 9, but with five not-outs among his 14 innings he could at least say the opposition found him hard to get rid of.

Away from the middle

His cricket took him well beyond Jharkhand. He signed for Durham in the English County Championship in 2014, and in the Indian Premier League he was signed by Kings XI Punjab, Rajasthan Royals and Gujarat Titans. In 2018 and 2019 he was picked for India B and India Red in the national competitions.

He stepped away from first-class cricket in February 2024, and in July 2025 Sunrisers Hyderabad made him their fast bowling coach. The next generation of quick bowlers could hardly ask for someone who knows the job better.

And finally

Not many bowlers have a speed in their record that ends in a decimal point. Varun Aaron's 153.4 km/h was the kind of number that batsmen remember for years, usually while rubbing a bruise.
